title: Canada's prison service failed Edward Snowshoe as it did Ashley Smith: Editorial
subtitle: It's as if Canada learned nothing from Ashley Smith's tragic death - an inquiry has concluded another federal inmate, Edward Snowshoe, committed suicide amid official neglect.
article: Their backgrounds could hardly have been more different - but their death was very much the same. Ashley Smith and Edward Snowshoe both killed themselves in federal prison, in both cases after a cruelly long period of segregation and while overseen by guards who failed to do their duty.

The miscarriage of justice was so profound in Smith's case that an inquest jury described her death as a homicide. And an inquiry into Snowshoe's suicide concluded this past week that he died because he "fell through the cracks" of the system.

In a testament to the appalling inertia within the Correctional Service of Canada, Snowshoe hanged himself in custody almost three years after Smith's choking death in 2007. It was as if nothing had been learned from one of the most horrific examples of institutional failure in Canadian history.

The mistreatment to which Smith was subjected has become notorious, and rightly so. In light of her fate, corrections officials should have mended systemic "cracks" through which an inmate could fatally drop. But Snowshoe was allowed to fall anyway.

This 24-year-old from Fort McPherson, N.W.T., was serving a 51⁄2-year sentence for the armed robbery of a cab driver in which the cabbie was hurt. Snowshoe endured a difficult incarceration that ended when he spent a stretch of 162 days in segregation and then committed suicide on Aug. 13, 2010.

He was held in isolation from the general population for 134 of those days at the Stony Mountain Institution in Manitoba, after being caught with a makeshift "knife" fashioned out of a juice box. Snowshoe was then transferred to the maximum security Edmonton Institution where segregation continued for another 28 days. That's where, overwhelmed by despair, he killed himself.

Alberta Judge James Wheatley conducted an inquiry into this death and his report Tuesday revealed a tragic string of oversights and mix-ups. There were clear signals that Snowshoe was at serious risk, including that he had tried to kill himself three times at Stony Mountain where he had been put on suicide watch. But corrections officials in Edmonton either weren't aware of this history or failed to take it into account. As a result, Snowshoe wasn't appropriately monitored.

There was confusion over whether he belonged in segregation at all. Instead of being subject to a proper and thorough review, Snowshoe's segregation clock was simply reset on his arrival in Edmonton - it was started anew, with officials unaware of exactly how long he had already spent in isolation in Manitoba.

Ironically, Edmonton jail guards could have learned a great deal about Snowshoe's mental state and incarceration history had they consulted a corrections system database called the Offender Management System. But those in charge of Snowshoe simply weren't aware of it. He paid for these failures with his life.

All this would have been bad enough under any circumstances, but it's utterly inexcusable given that it came three years after Smith's passing, and in a modern era when prison authorities should have been better prepared to cope with these cases. Smith choked herself with a strip of cloth in a Kitchener prison while guards watched. Before that she traced a ghastly journey through Canada's incarceration system , including being drugged against her will, hooded, shackled and even duct-taped into submission. Smith endured 17 transfers and almost constant segregation before she died at the age of 19.

Her case and that of Snowshoe share tragic features: both involve prisoners rendered highly vulnerable by mental health problems - both were allowed to kill themselves through a series of bureaucratic foul-ups, mixed messages and fundamental uncaring.

Things have changed in very recent years, for the better. But the Snowshoe inquiry report is another searing, cautionary reminder that there's no room for complacency. Prisoners struggling with mental health issues need support and must receive it.
